page: Microsoft Azure FX64mds_v2 is a high-frequency compute- and memory-intensive virtual machine built on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. The instance is powered by an x86_64 Intel Xeon 8573C processor running at a clock speed of 4.2 GHz. It provides 64 dedicated vCPUs mapped across 32 physical cores with multithreading enabled. The CPU configuration features 48 KB of L1 data cache per core, 2 MB of L2 cache per core, and a shared 260 MB L3 cache pool. Hardware-level acceleration includes AVX-512 extensions and Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX), covering both amx_tile and amx_int8 execution units for vectorized matrix operations.

Resource allocation is characterized by an extensive memory footprint and bundled high-speed storage. The server provides 1344.0 GB of system memory, yielding 21.0 GB of RAM per virtual processor. Bundled local storage includes a 3780 GB NVMe solid-state drive, removing the need to rely exclusively on remote volumes for low-latency scratch space. The instance does not include GPU accelerators and provisions zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses by default.

Benchmark measurements highlight strong computational throughput and memory subsystem capacity. In synthetic evaluations, the host achieved a PassMark CPU score of 85,402.59 (top 10%) and a multi-core stress-ng metric of 70,926.61. Large-block uncached memory read bandwidth reached 392.4 GB/sec, while write operations attained 170.98 GB/sec, placing it in the top decile. In database operations, the instance scored 37,190.82 in PassMark tests and sustained 95.28 million Redis SET operations per second, supported by static web throughput measuring 97.07 GB/sec.

The dense pairing of 4.2 GHz clock frequencies, large L3 cache, substantial memory density, and local NVMe storage addresses tasks requiring heavy data throughput and high core speeds. Tradeoffs include standard single-thread baseline execution scores (stress-ng single-core index of 2171.29) and the absence of discrete accelerator hardware. The server fits in-memory database deployments, electronic design automation (EDA), compute-bound financial simulation, analytics pipelines, and data-intensive compilation workloads.
